Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

sense noun

good sense, judgement

also common sense, good sense, sensible, come to one’s senses, brains, she’s got brains, have common sense, you have no common sense at all, be sensible

classical

Cic. Off. 1.153: prūdentia … est rērum expetendārum fugiendārumque scientia

prūdentia, prūdentiae f.

noun, first declension · Declension on Wiktionary

good sense, practical judgement

Lewis & Short: “sagacity, good sense, intelligence, prudence, practical judgment”.

Other words

  • sapiō, sapere, sapīvī — have sense, be sensible

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Ps. 240: Nunc tū sapis.; Mart. 13.5.2: sī sapis, adde piper; Traupman 157 · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Sī sapis, if you have any sense.

  • sēnsus commūnis — common sense

    also used · classical · Phaedr. 1.7.4: sēnsum commūnem abstulit

    Plain common sense in Phaedrus; in Cicero and Horace rather tact, a feeling for others (Lewis & Short).

  • bona mēns — good sense, a sound mind

    also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 27.8: bona mēns nec commodātur nec emitur; Petron. 61.1: bonam mentem bonamque valētūdinem

  • resipīscō, resipīscere, resipīvī — come to one’s senses

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Ter. Heaut. 842–844; Cic. Att. 4.5.1 (Lewis & Short); de Vaan 538, s.v. sapiō · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Lewis & Short: “to recover one’s senses, come to one’s self again … become reasonable”.

  • cor, cordis n. — sense, wits: the heart as the seat of the mind

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cato in Liv. Epit. 50: eam lēgātiōnem nec caput nec pedēs nec cor habēre (Lewis & Short s.v. pēs); Traupman 93, 95; Traupman 294: cor habēre · Declension on Wiktionary

    Lewis & Short: the heart as “understanding, mind, judgment”, most frequent in the early poets. Cor habēre, to have sense.

  • corcillum, corcillī n. — a little heart; brains

    noun, second declension · also used · post-classical · Petr. 75: corcillum est quod hominēs facit (Lewis & Short); Traupman 94 · Declension on Wiktionary

    (vōx sermōnis vulgāris: Petr.)

Examples

  • Manē, manē, jam ut volēs mēd esse ita erō. — Nunc tū sapis.

    Wait, wait, I’ll be just as you want me. — Now you’re talking sense.Plaut. Ps. 240

  • bona mēns nec commodātur nec emitur

    Good sense can be neither borrowed nor bought.Sen. Ep. 27.8

  • Hoc illīs dictum est, quibus honōrem et glōriam Fortūna tribuit, sēnsum commūnem abstulit.

    This is said for those to whom Fortune has given honour and glory, and taken away common sense.Phaedr. 1.7.3–4

  • Nōn cor omnīnō habēs.

    You have no common sense at all.Traupman 93

  • Corcillum habet.

    She’s got brains.Traupman 94

See also mind, clever, silly, sense.
